title: Litigation means and policy ends
gist: DAT Green analyses Meta’s $18bn settlement with several US state governments over claims its products harmed children, arguing the binding platform changes it forces are welcome but that governing corporations by litigation settlement rather than by democratic rule-making is a problematic and arguably undemocratic sign that the normal policy process is broken.

insights.claim: Meta agreed an $18bn settlement in the US with several state governments to resolve claims its products harmed children.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Sets a benchmark for the scale of legal exposure social platforms now face over child-safety claims.
insights.locator: The settlement this week between the Meta corporation

insights.claim: Green argues the settlement’s real significance is not the money—relatively insignificant for Meta—but that it legally binds Meta to make wide-ranging platform and product changes it had long resisted.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The binding product obligations, not the cash, are the material outcome for how platforms operate.
insights.quote: The significance of the deal is not the monies that will be paid

insights.claim: State governments benefited from an evidence base of internal Meta warnings about addiction risks, which Green likens to the adverse evidence in historic tobacco litigation and suggests Meta did not want explained to a jury.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Internal-document exposure is the recurring lever that forces tech firms to settle rather than litigate.
insights.locator: In the Meta litigation the state governments

insights.claim: Green stresses that breaching a court-sanctioned settlement is effectively a contempt of court and can be enforced swiftly—unlike defying a mere statutory duty—making settlement obligations bite harder and faster.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Explains why a settlement can compel corporate behaviour change more effectively than legislation.
insights.quote: A breach of such an agreement is effectively a contempt of court.

insights.claim: Green argues implementing public policy through settlement agreements is problematic and arguably undemocratic because settlements are private agreements, not public judgments or democratically accountable rules.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Frames the core governance risk: major policy outcomes set by deal-making outside democratic accountability.
insights.quote: This is administration by deal-making, and not by rule-making or policy-making.
insights.locator: But before we all clap and cheer

insights.claim: Green warns litigation is an inexact tool whose dynamics are hard to control—hard-fought cases can go any direction and settlement terms depend on last-minute contingencies and negotiating leverage.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Cautions that policy outcomes achieved by litigation are unpredictable and not reliably reproducible.
insights.locator: But litigation is an inexact activity

insights.claim: Green contends corporations are adept at lobbying politicians and influencing elections to resist changes upstream in the policy process, which is precisely why litigation becomes the only remaining route to force change.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Identifies regulatory-lobbying capture as the root cause pushing reform into the courts.
insights.locator: But the problem with this ideal approach

insights.claim: Green notes settlements are not always benign, citing President Trump’s recent use of a compromise agreement to try to force through a fund for paying political supporters—showing the same mechanism can be abused to make law by other means.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Warns the settlement mechanism is politically neutral and can serve illegitimate ends as easily as legitimate ones.
insights.locator: And settlements are not always good things.

insights.claim: Green’s conclusion is that the most significant fact in the Meta case is not that Meta may have broken the law but that the democratic system itself is broken, leaving welcome ends achieved by problematic means.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The essay’s central diagnosis: reliance on litigation settlements signals a failure of democratic rule-making.
insights.quote: the democratic system is itself broken
